I have an amendment to offer with respect to the rate of interest to be paid as a rental by the Grand Trunk Pacific for the use of the eastern section under this agreement. While it is quite specifically defined in this agreement that the lease shall be at the rate of 3 per cent on the total cost to the country of the construction of the road, we are left at sea as to what that cost will amount to to the country. We know that the money for its construction will have to be borrowed, and yet even with the conditions the best that have ever been known Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
in Canada, money cannot be borrowed at that rate, and it is not conceivable that when the Canadian government enters into such a huge speculation, shall I call it, as the building of this road, taking into consideration all its conditions and all its probabilities, Canadian credit is likely to improve to such an extent that money will be procurable at a lower rate than it is to-day ; the probabilities apj)ear rather to be in the opposite direction. It is not likely that for years to come at any rate we shall be able under the very best conditions to borrow money at 3 per cent, which is the rate fixed at which the Grand Trunk shall pay for the road. I offer all amendment to it as follows, seconded by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson) :
Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the Act amended, or in the scheduled agreements contained, the rental to be paid by the Pacific Company in respect of the eastern division under the lease thereof shall be payable half-yearly and shall not be less than the average rate of interest payable from time to time upon the moneys borrowed by the government for the construction of the eastern division.
In offering this amendment I am fully conscious of the fact that having already come under the consideration of this parliament it is not likely to be carried now, but we on this side of the House feel it our duty to emphatically and as clearly as we can, place ourselves on record as to what our views are on this very important arrangement which has been entered into between the government of Canada, the people of Canada and the Grand Trunk Railway Company. This apparently insignificant difference between 3 per cent and 3* per cent which is the best rate at which we can procure money, totals up a very large item on the total cost of the road, and for the whole period for which the Grand Trunk will have the privilege of practically owning it for the nominal payment of a rental. It does seem a reasonable and fair thing that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should pay at least as much rental as the government has to pay for the money which they borrow. Taking into consideration all the privileges that are granted to this company and all the advantages that are given to them under this contract, in the original contract and in the improved conditions which they have got under the amendments which have been suggested and added thereto by the Grand Trunk themselves, it seems to me that this apparently small concession should be made by that company. It may seem small, but it is a very important one, running up into millions of dollars. It is estimated by the great railway expert of this country, that there is a difference of some $18,000,000, possibly more than that under the improved conditions in favour of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and therefore it seems that they should be compelled to

pay for the rental of the eastern division at least at the same rate of interest that it would cost the country to borrow the money for the extension. .
Then, Sir, while the provision is made in the contract that the rental is to be paid over to the government annually at a certain time of the year it would be but reasonable that being in possession of the road continually and deriving revenue from it constantly they should at least pay that interest half yearly. This would be an important difference to the exchequer and a provision of this kind should we think be embodied in the Bill. If this is not adopted at least we shall have the satisfaction of knowing that we have asked from the government on behalf of the people of Canada that which seems to be a reasonable and fair thing, and one which should be conceded in all fairness to the country in view of the extensive . privileges granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific in respect to this part of the contract. In asking the concession of these two points, the payment of rental half yearly and the payment of a rate of interest at least equivalent to the average cost to the country of the borrowed money, we are simply asking what should be done in justice to the people of Canada. As I said before we may not succeed in having these amendments carried, but we feel that tlie country should know that we as representatives of various sections of Canada have been voicing our views of what is fair and just, and we believe that in doing so we are voicing the opinions of the mass of the electors who are behind us and to whom we have to give an account of our stewardship. We believe that these very reasonable amendments will meet with the approval and the endorsation of the mass of the people who think on these matters irrespective of any political bias which they may have. Therefore, I would submit this amendment to the House without any further discussion.
Mr. FITZPATRICK, In reference to this amendment as well as to that moved by my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) I beg to say that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) who is especially charged with the financial arrangements of the government, dealt with that question from the financial standpoint in committee, and I should prefer to echo here merely what he said at that time and assume that what he said would be the answer for the government if he were present at this time.

I think this is a very reasonable amendment and one which will receive the support of the country if it does not receive the support of this House. I do not see why we should be called upon to construct the eastern section of this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, borrow the money, possibly, at three and a half per cent, assume all the responsibility and risk in connection with this expenditure and then give the road over to the company at a rental which shall be less than the rate which we have to pay in interest. 1 believe that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should pay the government in rent what the interest will cost us. It is not likely that this country will be able to borrow money for years to come at any better rate than we are borrowing at today. The government cannot borrow money to-day at three per cent. With the increased demand for money by the government of Canada, with the liabilities which will have to be met from time to time and with the increasing requirements of this country it must be that our credit will not stand as well in the future as it has in the past. I believe that we will have to pay considerably more than three per cent for the money which is required to construct the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. I do; not see why we should be asked to pay a greater rate of interest than we ask the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to pay for the use of the road. That being the case I think this is a reasonable amendment and one that ought to commend itself to every member of this House, as I am satisfied that it will commend itself to the country. I therefore shall have much pleasure in supporting this amendment.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) has so set his face against reason and the amendments up to this time that I have somewhat despaired of the hon. gentleman acceding to anything that was even so completely within the bounds of reason that it would be difficult to find a justification for his resistance. I beg leave to move the following amendment:
That the Bill he not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions to add the following section thereto : -
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause 3 of the supplementary agreement it is hereby provided that in the event of the completion of that portion of the eastern division which shall extend from a point at or near Winnipeg easterly to the point of junction with the Pacific Company's branch line to Lake Superior, or easterly to the point of junction with the Pacific Company's branch line to North Bay, before the completion by the Dominion of Canada of the -whole eastern division, then the Pacific Company shall he entitled to lease, and shall lease, pending such full completion, from the commissioners the said portion and portions so constructed from a point at or near Winnipeg to such points of junction, at and subject to a rental, payable halfyearly, equal to 3 per cent per annum upon the cost of construction of the said portion or por-

tions so leased, and subject also to such reasonable and usual conditions as may be agreed between the commissioners and the Pacific Company ; provided that the said lease or leases shall be subject always to the paramount right of the said commissioners to use and operate the whole or any part of the said portions so leased, and for such purposes as they may deem necessary or expedient in the execution of their commission ; and the commissioner shall allow and deduct from the rents so to be paid by the Pacific Company reasonable tolls or compensation for their exercise from time to time of the right to such use and operation, which tolls or compensation may be agreed between the Paeifi.c Company and the commissioners, and in case of failure to agree as to the same, or as to the aforesaid, conditions of the lease, they shall be determined in the manner provided by paragraph 24 (2) of the agreement aforesaid.
I can scarcely believe that it was present to the minds of the members of the government that under the agreement the Pacific Company would have the use of that line during the whole period of construction free from any rent or tolls, and that they would after the completion of the whole of the eastern line be entitled to enter into possession under the general lease which practically covers ten years without any payment of rent. The hon. Minister of Justice told us, I think, only a day or two ago, that it was the intention of the government to construct the eastern section simultaneously with the western section ; that would mean the completion of the whole of the western section, including the mountain section which covers a period of eight years. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company construct the western section, as has been strongly represented by hon. gentlemen opposite and more especially by the hon. Minister of Justice himself, within a very short period there is absolu-tely\ no doubt that the sections from Winnipeg to Fort William, or some portion of Lake Superior will be constructed in order that the water route may be used, and to North Bay in order that there may be connection had with the old Grand Trunk system through the province of Ontario, using practically their own system as far as the east is concerned. I can scarcely believe that the members of the government had that called to their attention, or if they had, that they would not have remedied what seems to be a great defect. There is no reason why the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should not pay rent for that. On the other hand there is very great reason why they should pay for it because they use it and will use it probably as a spout from the west even after the eastern section is constructed. It would amount under ordinary conditions to this, that they would have a portion of the road for at least eighteen years, if it took eight years to construct the western section free of rent. It would have another effect. Hon.

gentlemen opposite had laid much stress upon the fact that the line which ia going to be built from Winnipeg to Quebec and to Moncton will be a guarantee that Canadian products will be carried through Canadian ports. Hon. gentlemen opposite can see that the moment that the eastern section is constructed from, say, North Bay, or Fort William, or both, the whole of the traffic will go over the two branch lines. During the season of navigation the Grand Trunk Pacific will avail of the water route just as the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern do now, and when navigation closes the tendency will be for the Grand Trunk Railway to bring this western freight to Portland over their own line. I do not know that we can enter into a quarrel with a great railway corporation because they conduct their business on strict business principles, and that is what the Grand Trunk Railway would be doing if they sent their freight to Portland. If the Minister of Justice were making this agreement anew, I doubt if he would provide that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company should have that line during the whole term of construction on the terms provided for in this clause. I do not think that the Minister of Justice will now say that that provision is in the interest of Canada. I do not yet despair that the hon. gentleman will accept this amendment, which indeed hardly goes far enough to provide a reasonable safeguard in the public interest.
I can well understand why the Minister of Justice does not like to accept all these amendments. Why, he would not know his own child to morrow if he were to dress it up in these amendments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The child would be so much better looking, that the Minister of Justice would think that it did not belong to himself. The prairie section will be finished first, and the Grand Trunk will be anxious to get from Winnipeg to Port Arthur and North Bay so that they may be in a position to route the grain over their own system to Portland. The longer that state of things prevails the more difficult it will be to get the freight over your eastern section when it is completed to Quebec. It is generally understood that the ocean freight rates largely control the routing of export freight, and for years freights have been cheaper from (Portland than from our Canadian ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not for wheat.
In winter ?

speechtext: In summer.

I am sure the Minister of Justice will see the reasonableness of the amendment, so that the Grand Trunk Paci-

fic may have to make some further arrangement with the commissioners in order to control that traffic previous to the eastern section being completed. I trust the hon. gentleman will accept this safeguard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The difference between our hon. friends and ourselves is, that in the contemplation of the government the eastern extension is to run from Winnipeg to Moncton, whereas in the contemplation of hon. gentlemen opposite, the eastern section is to run to North Bay and never go further. The government, by the amendment to the original contract, provides that the completed portions of the eastern section may at any time be let by the commissioners to the Grand Trunk Pacific, but hon. gentlemen opposite want to make this power applicable exclusively to that part of the line between North Bay and Winnipeg. My hon. friends must remember that this is the point at issue between us ; that is their policy as against ours. The policy which hon. gentlemen opposite have, is the extension of the Grand Trunk system from North Bay to Winnipeg ; our policy is the construction of the road from Winnipeg to Quebec and Moncton. So long as we are at issue on this point, my hon. friends cannot expect, with reason, that we should accept this amendment, which would have the effect of defeating the whole policy of the government. My hon. friends' oppo-s te say that the road frem Winnipeg lo North Bay will be constructed first. I do not agree that anything of the sort is to take place. I apprehend that the whole road is to be constructed simultaneously. Even if the road is constructed from Winnipeg to a point north of North Bay, I cannot see any obj ction whatever to the commissioners leasing that part of the line to the Grand T.unk Pacific Company. We have no desire to prevent the trade going to North Bay if that is the natural channel-
Is it the intention of the government that in such an event the Grand Trunk Pacific shall pay rental ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, it is , and that is what our agreement provides for. According to the amendment, if the commissioners lease a part of this road to the company, they shall be under an obligation to give it to them for seven years for nothing. On that point we are at variance with our hon. friends. We say that is a preposterous construction to put upon the terms of the agreement-that no such arrangement is in contemplation. All you would have to compare it with would be the lease of ihe "hole line.
And not more onerous ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not the lease that is to be more onerous ; it is the terms. What is to be compared is the lease of a part for a limited period with the lease of
1he whole line for fifty years ; and you have also to compare the lease of that part subject to the paramount right of the commissioners: So that it is impossible to provide at the present time for the terms of that lease, because no man can now foresee the extent to which the commissioners may use it or the partial use to be given to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ; and if you do not know the extent of the user, or the period, it is impossible to determine the conditions of the lease. All these things will be determined when the time comes to use the road, and when the conditions under which it is to be used are determined. I say this amendment puts in issue the two policies-the policy of the opposition, which is the extension of the Grand Trunk system from North Bay into the Northwest
No, no.

speechtext:
Oh, yes ; and against the policy of the government, which involves the construction of the eastern extension as one road from Winnipeg to Moncton.	.

Mr. Speaker, I have an amendment to the 7t!>
section, being in fact the same amendment which I had the honour of moving when the House was in Committee of the Whole. It reads as follows :
That the Bill he not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend the same .by adding to section 7 of the Bill, the following as subsection ' d ' :-
Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the Act hereby amended, or in the scheduled agreements contained, His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, conditions or stipulations in the said scheduled agreements contained on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, unless and until the Grand Trunk Company shall have entered into an agreement with His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, by which the said Grand Trunk Company shall covenant and agree as follows :-That neither the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company nor the Grand Trunk Company shall in any manner within its power, directly or indirectly, permit, advise or encourage the transportation of traffic bv routes or at rates other than those provided in the said agreement, and that each of the said companies shall, in all respects and in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted and accepted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and to Canadian ocean ports.
When this motion was moved in Committee of the Whole, the hon. Minister of Justice, in answer to the observations which l then had the honour of making upon it, said that it went upon the assumption that the Grand Trunk Company would be inteiested

in ruining the business of the Pacific Company. It appears to me to be a sufficient reply to that to say, as I in fact said when moving the amendment, that the two companies are the same entity, and, therefore, while the Grand Trunk Pacific may gather and receive the traffic in the west, that same interest, composed of the two companies, and being largely the same personnel, will, in any event, get possession of the traffic. It will b.e of no consequence to the joint railroad interest by what route the traffic shall reach the Atlantic, and therefore they will take it where the terminals and the ships are best provided. It appears to me that that is a sufficient answer to that objection. Unless this amendment is accepted, the Grand Trunk Company will remain unbound, as it is at present, to endeavour to route the traffic by the Pacific line. It will be at perfect liberty to take either, alternative route-by Chicago or by North Bay ; and both companies, being the same interest, so long as they get possession of the traffic, will take it by the route by which they will make the greatest amount of freight, and which will best answer the purpose of the service' they are performing for the public. But we are asking ill this amendment that not only shall the Pacific Company come under these agreements and be bound by both Bills, .but that the Grand Trunk Company shall enter into like covenants and be equally bound. Thr Minister of Justice also objected that it was not shown that there were any American connections by which the traffic could be sent by way of Chicago. I am informed, and I have heard it frequently asserted in this House, that there are American lines in which the Grand Trunk Company is interested, which can be connected by a short link of some sixty miles, by which Chicago can be reached by the Grand Trunk from Winnipeg. A further objection which the hon. minister urged was that the Grand Trunk Railway have to guarantee the second issue of Grand Trunk Pacific bonds, and he asks how will they pay the interest on thosr bonds if they ruin the earning capacity of the Grand Trunk Pacific. In reply allow me to observe again that the companies are practically one. Even the personnel of the companies is, to a large extent, one and having the same interest, the same observations apply to what is in fact the same objection.
Another answer by my hon. friend was that the Grand Trunk Railway will hold the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific and must pay for it, and having paid money for it, he again asks will they ruin the earning capacity of the company whose stock they hold ? This point has been debated at very great length during the various stages of this measure, both in the Bill of last year and that presented this year. On the government side it has been persistently urged that this stock must and will be paid for by the Grand Trunk Rail-Mr. ALCORN.
way ; but if we turn to the agreement we find that the covenant into which the Grand Trunk Railway enters is not that it will acquire and pay for this stock. It it not that that company will purchase it as an ordinary purchaser. The words used are that it will ' receive and take.' Surely there is no imputation there that it will pay cash at the market or any other price. Had that been the intention, had both the government and the Grand Trunk Railway meant purchase, surely some such words as ' purchase and acquire ' or ' purchase and pay for ' would have been used instead of the words ' receive and take.' In my experience, I have never known that when it was intended to bind a person to pay for a thing, he was simply requested to receive and take it. And we have a formal notice, in the most explicit terms, given us by the president of the Grand Trunk Railway, that this construction of the contract is the one on which he intends his company shall act, and that they will take this stock as a consideration for guaranteeing the second issue of bonds and will not pay for it. If that is their idea of the obligation. Once that stock is transferred to them in consideration of their guaranteeing the bonds, it will become their property, and it follows as a matter of course that whatever money consideration they may obtain for it, when they dispose of that stock, will go into the coffers of the Grand Trunk Railway and never become the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific. These appear to me sufficient answers to the objections stated by the hon. minister to this amendment. I am not disposed to go again over the arguments forming the grounds which I have already assigned as the proper ground on which the minister could accept this amendment, and I leave the matter with these observations in the strong hope that further consideration will induce the hon. minister to accept the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend proceeds on the assumption that the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway will be at variance with those of the Grand Trunk Pacific. In the view of the government, they will be identical. They will be identical, in the first place, because the Grand Trunk Railway will guarantee the second issue of bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and in the second place because the Grand Trunk Railway will hold over $22,000,000 of the common stock of the latter company, for which it must pay either money or money's worth. My hon. friend is not quite correct in assuming that I at any time said that the Grand Trunk Railway was under obligations to pay cash for this stock. What I said was that it was obliged to pay cash or its equivalent. My hon. friend must bear in mind in addition that the Grand Trunk Railway, at its very inception, sought

to obtain connection with the Northwest through North Bay and in that way to Winnipeg. Any failure on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry out any part of its obligations, and the whole of the eastern section is to be dealt with and operated as a whole, will cause the lease to be inoperative. These are the reasons why the amendment is not necessary. It would be idle to go over them again. I cannot convince my hon friend, and I am sure he has not convinced me. and I must ask the House to reject the amendment.

The interests of the Grand Trunk Railway may be the same as those of the Grand Trunk Pacific, so far as the eastern section is concerned, but possibly they may not. A condition of affairs might arise, under which it would be more in the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway to send its freight by some other route than by the eastern division. That is not at all impossible. In the first place, the Grand Trunk Railway at some future time may be able, by the exercise of the same influence which has procured these concessions, to get rid of the eastern division. or have the terms of the lease modified. In that case one can readily see that any safeguard arising from the necessity of their using the eastern division is absolutely gone, but if you have the Grand Trunk Railway bound by a stipulation in this contract, while you may not obtain a perfect safeguard, you have a very much better one than at present. This is exactly in the line of the amendment voted down not many minutes ago by which we sought to place upon the statutes the declaration that parliament can be invoked if the Grand Trunk Railway should not in good faith carry out the stipulations of this contract, although not formally bound by it. This amendment attempts to accomplish the same object by another means, namely, by imposing directly on the Grand Trunk Railway stipulations in the contract which are at present only legally binding on the Grand Trunk Pacific. In this view, while we do not wish to emj)liasize the fact that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has not convinced us, nevertheless we must persevere in our amendment and ask the vote of the House upon it.
